bridges.description: Whether the universe’s beginning, apparent design, and moral truths together are best explained by a supreme being.
Whether a beginning of the universe calls for a cause beyond space, time, and matter.
Whether life-permitting order is best explained by an intelligent source.
Whether objective moral truths require a grounding explanation and whether God supplies it.
Whether abductive comparison can identify God as the best explanation without claiming certainty.
Whether the offered case leaves God unproved and critical nonbelief justified.
Whether the proposed spaceless, timeless, immaterial personal cause is coherent.
Whether natural selection, variable constants, or a multiverse undercut the design inference.
Whether moral values arise in minds while consequences can still be assessed objectively.
Whether the affirmative has supplied enough evidence and argument to meet its burden.

sections.title: Burden, evidence, and qualified belief
sections.rationale: Frames what each side says the motion requires and how a cumulative but uncertain case bears on justified belief.

sections.title: Cosmic origin and causal explanation
sections.rationale: Covers the beginning-of-the-universe argument and objections about causation, time, and power.

sections.title: Design, fine-tuning, and alternatives
sections.rationale: Addresses the intelligent-design inference and the competing multiverse and observer-selection explanations.

sections.title: Morality, minds, and grounding
sections.rationale: Covers whether moral truths are mind-independent, how harm grounds assessment, and whether God explains morality.

sections.title: Coherence and explanatory method
sections.rationale: Addresses the proposed divine attributes and whether best-explanation reasoning is legitimate rather than gap-filling.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The universe had a beginning and therefore had a cause.
moves.warrant: Whatever has a beginning must have a cause, and the universe had a beginning.
moves.inference: A cause of the universe is required.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest contiguous passage containing both premises and the stated conclusion of Johnson’s first-cause argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: therefore the universe had a cause
moves.attributionRationale: The passage falls within Johnson’s uninterrupted opening after his named handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: This is one of the three principal constructive lines in the cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the causal premise for moving from cosmic beginning to a transcendent explanation.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: A supreme being is offered as the best explanation of the universe’s cause.
moves.warrant: Johnson proposes abductive reasoning that compares possible explanations for an observed effect.
moves.inference: The causal argument is presented as an inference to the best explanation rather than a deductive identification of God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Johnson’s distinction between a cause and God and ends after he defines the abductive method he will use.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is part of Johnson’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the inferential method governing the whole cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It links the observed effects to the proposed theistic explanation while preserving the explanatory burden.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The cause of the universe is reasonably characterized as spaceless, timeless, immaterial, and powerful.
moves.warrant: Johnson says the universe consists of space, time, and matter, so a cause preceding their beginning would not itself be spatial, temporal, or material; causing a universe also indicates power.
moves.inference: The first cause has attributes associated with a supreme being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This immediately follows the causal syllogism and contains Johnson’s complete causal-to-divine attribute bridge.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: this cause is very powerful
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Johnson’s uninterrupted opening and uses clear wording outside the later recognition-caution ranges.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the necessary bridge from a generic cause to the kind of cause relevant to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the properties Johnson infers from causing space, time, and matter.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Evidence of design in the universe points to an intelligent designer.
moves.warrant: Johnson says observed design has only been seen to come from intelligent minds and that the universe displays fine-tuning.
moves.inference: The universe was designed by an intelligent mind.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains the two stated premises, conclusion, and Johnson’s short explanation of the analogy without importing surrounding citations.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: therefore the universe was designed by an intelligent mind
moves.attributionRationale: The argument appears in Johnson’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: Fine-tuning is a principal line of Johnson’s cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes the central inferential link from fine-tuning to intelligent agency.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: God is presented as the best explanation for objective moral truths.
moves.warrant: Johnson states that there are objective moral truths independent of human minds.
moves.inference: If God best explains those objective truths, God exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact span contains Johnson’s complete two-premise moral argument and stated conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: therefore god exists
moves.attributionRationale: This is the end of Johnson’s uninterrupted opening before the moderator handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: Moral grounding is one of the three principal constructive lines.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly connects claimed objective moral truth to the theistic conclusion.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The wrongness of abusing women does not change merely because everyone’s belief changes.
moves.warrant: Johnson asks whether universal belief produced by a pill would make abuse morally permissible and answers that it would not.
moves.inference: At least some moral truths are independent of human minds.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This focused span contains the complete moral case of the thought experiment without the earlier color and arithmetic setup.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's objectively wrong it's a truth independent of our minds
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Johnson’s uninterrupted opening and contains no noted recognition uncertainty.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides the principal support for the first premise of Johnson’s moral argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It supports the claim that moral truth requires an explanation beyond changing human belief.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Barker’s position is primarily absence of theistic belief rather than certainty that no god exists.
moves.warrant: He distinguishes hard atheists from most atheists and agnostics who lack belief.
moves.inference: His burden is critical assessment of the offered theistic case, not proof of universal divine nonexistence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage gives Barker’s operative definition before he develops the burden analogy.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: atheism is simply the absence of theism
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is within Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the qualified con position against which the motion is assessed.

burdenContact.rationale: It defines the con motion-level stance as lack of warranted belief.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Barker argues that the affirmative must make a case beyond reasonable doubt rather than requiring him to disprove every possible god.
moves.warrant: His elf analogy assigns the burden to the party asserting existence, and he notes that reasonable disagreement remains.
moves.inference: Showing that Johnson’s case fails to remove reasonable doubt is sufficient for Barker’s stated position.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage contains the burden question, the reasonable-doubt standard, and Barker’s qualified statement of what he must establish.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Barker’s uninterrupted opening after the named handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: This defines the con burden and governs how every objection bears on the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the standard under which the existence claim remains unproved.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The proposed spaceless and timeless being is not coherently defined.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that beings, agency, measurement, and existence ordinarily involve space and time, while the proposed definition removes those conditions.
moves.inference: A motion about such a being cannot get started until a coherent definition is supplied.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span captures Barker’s first stated lack and the complete married-bachelor analogy.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't even know what we're talking about
moves.attributionRationale: This is within Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: The objection challenges the intelligibility of the entity named in the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly contests whether the proposed divine attributes form a coherent object of belief.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether the inferred spaceless, timeless, immaterial cause is a coherent being.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: For a god defined as both omniscient and freely choosing, foreknowledge of its own future removes the uncertainty Barker says choice requires.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that choice requires options and a period of uncertainty, while an omniscient god already knows what it will do.
moves.inference: That specific combination of omniscience and free will is incoherent, though other definitions of god may escape the objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Barker’s complete FANG argument and his explicit qualification that other god definitions might be formulated.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if you know the future you cannot have free will
moves.attributionRationale: The argument is clearly owned by Barker in his uninterrupted opening; the corrected frozen notes confirm its meaning.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a developed conceptual objection to a prominent god definition, qualified rather than universalized.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests the joint coherence of omniscience and divine free choice.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The lack of strong public evidence makes nonbelief reasonable.
moves.warrant: Barker contrasts cultural stories and images with good evidence and says a genuinely demonstrated unknown cosmic force would attract scientific recognition.
moves.inference: The continued need to debate and infer God is evidence of an evidential absence, though not a disproof.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span runs from Barker’s second stated lack through his qualified conclusion that the debate itself illustrates missing evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i'm not saying this disproves god
moves.attributionRationale: This is in Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: The evidence challenge directly contacts Barker’s burden and the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the public evidence offered does not meet the affirmative burden.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Fine-tuning mistakes adaptation to the universe for evidence that the universe was designed for us.
moves.warrant: Barker says organisms are fine-tuned to the universe and uses reversed-premise analogies involving borders and rivers and noses and glasses.
moves.inference: Observed fit does not by itself establish prior intelligent design.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest continuous passage containing the stated reversal and the analogies used to explain it.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we are fine-tuned for the universe
moves.attributionRationale: The reply is within Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly targets one of Johnson’s three main arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers adaptation as an alternative account of apparent fit.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the direction of the design inference by treating organisms as adapted to the universe.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Unexplained features should not be filled with a familiar god hypothesis.
moves.warrant: Barker notes that past agency explanations for thunder gave way to natural explanations and that current science still has unanswered questions.
moves.inference: A gap in present knowledge is not positive evidence for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the god-of-the-gaps charge, its historical illustration, and Barker’s acknowledgment of current open questions.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are many unanswered questions
moves.attributionRationale: The move is in Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the explanatory method used across the affirmative’s cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that explanatory ignorance does not discharge the affirmative burden.

responseComponents.description: Argues that unexplained effects cannot by themselves establish the proposed theistic explanation.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Theists’ disagreement about God and moral issues weakens the claim that theism supplies clear guidance.
moves.warrant: Barker notes disagreement among believers about God’s nature and about major moral questions.
moves.inference: Religious disagreement counts among the absences supporting his critical position.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Barker’s complete fourth-lack argument, from the stated lack of agreement through the question why there is not one religion.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage lies in Barker’s uninterrupted opening and contains clear speaker ownership.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a developed but subsidiary line later answered independently in Johnson’s closing.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents disagreement as evidence that the claimed source has not yielded clear, shared guidance.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: People can live moral lives without belief in God, and morality can be oriented toward avoiding harm.
moves.warrant: Barker points to nonbelievers’ meaningful moral lives and describes moral practice through the intention to avoid harm in the real world.
moves.inference: A god is not needed for moral conduct or practical moral assessment.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Barker’s final stated lack and his qualified conclusion that nonbelief is justified rather than proved.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it is justifiable it's not proof but it is justifiable not to hold a belief in a god
moves.attributionRationale: This closes Barker’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a con alternative account relevant to the moral route while preserving the distinction from strict disproof.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds practical morality in real-world harm rather than a divine source.

responseComponents.description: Offers harm avoidance and lived moral practice as a non-theistic account of morality.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Varying multiple constants can permit other forms of life, and a multiverse is an alternative hypothesis under the same abductive method.
moves.warrant: Barker says more than one constant can change in compensating ways and explicitly proposes a multiverse as another explanatory candidate.
moves.inference: The life-permitting conditions do not uniquely identify an intelligent designer.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span retains the clear multiple-constant and alternative-hypothesis claims and stops before the recognition-corrupted firing-squad illustration.
moves.attributionRationale: The entire passage belongs to Barker’s uninterrupted rebuttal; the selected claim avoids the source-noted corrupted numerical wording.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Barker’s developed alternative to the design argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies alternative hypotheses and observer selection against uniqueness of design.

responseComponents.description: Argues that varying several constants and observer selection can yield life-permitting observations without design.
Uses the same abductive form to place a multiverse among candidate explanations.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Observers necessarily find themselves in a life-permitting universe, and such observations would look the same with or without a designer.
moves.warrant: Barker invokes the weak anthropic principle and says any observer must exist where observers are permitted.
moves.inference: The observation of life-permitting conditions does not discriminate between God and a non-theistic cosmos.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact span resumes after the recognition-corrupted numerical illustration and contains the unambiguous observer-selection conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: any observer obviously obviously is going to exist in the universe that permits observers to exist
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is clearly Barker’s rebuttal and avoids every restricted numerical clause.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides the epistemic link between the alternative hypothesis and the observed fine-tuning data.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that life-permitting observation is expected conditional on observers and so is not uniquely theistic.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the claim that observed life-permitting conditions uniquely indicate design.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Values are functions of minds rather than objects existing independently of brains.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that treating a value as an objective thing reifies a concept and that values arise through organisms interacting in the natural world.
moves.inference: The existence of moral valuation does not itself establish a mind-independent moral object.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Barker’s complete reification objection and mind-dependent account before he turns to bodily-function analogies.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a value is a function of a brain
moves.attributionRationale: The argument is within Barker’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Barker’s fullest answer to the moral-grounding argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the con account of values and objective moral assessment.

responseComponents.description: Rejects mind-independent values while preserving objective assessment of harm.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Moral choices can be assessed objectively by their real-world harm even though values exist in minds.
moves.warrant: Barker defines morality in terms of minimizing harm and says physical and psychological harm affect living organisms and can be evaluated.
moves.inference: Objective moral assessment does not require values to exist as mind-independent objects.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Barker’s complete harm-based account and its distinction between chosen values and objective real-world assessment.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: morality simply boils down to the intention to act with the minimal amount of harm
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is within Barker’s uninterrupted rebuttal and contains no restricted recognition wording.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the constructive alternative supporting Barker’s answer to the moral-grounding case.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how mind-dependent values can still guide objective consequence assessment.

responseComponents.description: Offers harm assessment as a non-theistic account of moral judgment.
Distinguishes objective verification of consequences from mind-independent moral objects.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The first-cause premise assumes a class of things that do not begin to exist and thereby imports its conclusion.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that experience supplies no example of things that do not begin to exist against which beginning things can be contrasted.
moves.inference: The cosmological argument does not independently establish God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete closing segment of Barker’s rebuttal devoted to the cosmological premise.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you are importing your conclusion into your premise
moves.attributionRationale: The passage remains within Barker’s uninterrupted rebuttal before applause.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly attacks another principal affirmative argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the cosmological premise cannot carry the affirmative burden without assuming the disputed conclusion.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the premise that partitions reality into beginning and non-beginning things.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The moral argument concerns explaining objective moral truths, including those accepted by some atheist philosophers.
moves.warrant: Johnson points to atheist affirmation of objective moral truths and asks how such truths can exist.
moves.inference: God remains a candidate best explanation even if nonbelievers recognize moral truths.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Johnson’s return to the moral argument and ends with his explicit best-explanation claim.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator has handed the floor to Johnson for his uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It restores the precise grounding burden after Barker’s practical-morality reply.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes moral knowledge and conduct from the existence and explanation of objective truths.

responseComponents.description: Clarifies that atheists’ moral conduct is not the target of the grounding argument.
Reasserts the question of how objective moral truths exist.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Both theistic and natural gap-filling are mistakes; each observed effect should be assessed for its best explanation.
moves.warrant: Johnson accepts that past theistic gap claims gained natural explanations but denies that this entails every cause is natural.
moves.inference: Labeling the arguments as gap arguments does not answer their comparative explanatory claim.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Johnson’s concession, parallel warning, and explicit restatement of the explanatory method.
moves.attributionRationale: The move is in Johnson’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It defends the common method connecting all three constructive arguments to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends comparative explanation against the claim that God merely fills ignorance.

responseComponents.description: Accepts poor gap arguments but argues that natural causes cannot be assumed for every unexplained effect.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: God may feel hidden, yet Johnson maintains that the offered effects provide good evidence for God.
moves.warrant: He concedes that more evidence would be better and identifies the beginning, design, and morality arguments as observed effects with a proposed best explanation.
moves.inference: Hiddenness does not erase the cumulative evidential case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Johnson’s concession about hiddenness and his direct evidential response before he turns to speculation about reasons for limited evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i think there is a lot of good evidence for god
moves.attributionRationale: This is within Johnson’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly meets the absence-of-evidence line while preserving Johnson’s conceded limits.

burdenContact.rationale: It states how the three offered effects cumulatively bear on belief despite hiddenness.

responseComponents.description: Concedes the desire for more evidence but maintains that the three presented effects supply evidence.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Immaterial realities outside space and time are coherent because abstract objects, mathematical truths, and logical truths are examples.
moves.warrant: Johnson explicitly points to abstract objects and mathematical and logical truths as existing outside space and time.
moves.inference: Calling a divine being immaterial and beyond space-time is not by itself incoherent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest clear passage stating Johnson’s abstract-object reply; it begins after the noted dropped-negation risk and ends before the noted philosopher-attribution uncertainty.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are immaterial things that exist outside of space and time
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson owns the uninterrupted rebuttal, and the selected words are the unambiguous surrounding claim explicitly authorized by the source notes.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Barker’s central definition objection without relying on corrupted clauses.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the coherence of positing immaterial reality in the explanatory case.

responseComponents.description: Counters that immaterial, non-spatiotemporal realities are not inherently incoherent.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Effects produced through human minds support an analogy from organized effects to an intelligent designer.
moves.warrant: Johnson points to music and physical actions as effects of minds and says design has not been observed from a source other than an intelligent mind.
moves.inference: Fine-tuned order can reasonably be attributed to a mind analogous to human intelligence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This clear span contains the human-mind design analogy and stops before the source-noted recognition uncertainty at events 1629–1631.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we've never seen design come from any other source than an intelligent mind
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson owns the uninterrupted rebuttal, and the selected span avoids all recognition-caution clauses.
moves.importanceRationale: It develops the analogy underlying the fine-tuning inference and supplies the actual target of Barker’s closing mind-function reply.

burdenContact.rationale: It supports inferring an intelligent source from effects identified as design.

responseComponents.description: Argues by analogy that a mind can be inferred through the effects it produces.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Unseen causes can reasonably be inferred from observable effects.
moves.warrant: Johnson compares inferring other minds from behavior and historical events from surviving evidence.
moves.inference: God need not be directly observed if a contingent, life-permitting universe is evidentially explained by God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains the complete effects-to-unseen-cause analogy and its application to the universe, separate from earlier recognition-uncertain wording.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we infer what happened in history from the effects and the evidence that's left behind
moves.attributionRationale: The speaker and wording are clear within Johnson’s uninterrupted rebuttal and outside the specified corrupted clauses.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers the demand for direct observation and supports the design inference’s evidential form.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why indirect effects may bear on an unobserved designer.

responseComponents.description: Argues that indirect effects can constitute evidence even without direct observation.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: A multiverse is less simple than one designer and would itself face causal and fine-tuning questions.
moves.warrant: Johnson contrasts one unobservable designer with many unobservable universes, argues a multiverse would still require a first cause or infinite regress, and says a universe-producing mechanism could itself require design.
moves.inference: The multiverse does not displace the theistic explanation of fine-tuning.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Johnson’s complete three-part multiverse response and his concern that the objection could explain away any evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a multiverse would still seem to require fine tuning too
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Johnson’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Barker’s main alternative to fine-tuning.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the alternative preserves rather than removes the causal and design questions.

responseComponents.description: Argues that a multiverse has its own causal, fine-tuning, and over-explanation liabilities.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The moral argument does not deny that atheists can act morally or know moral truths; it asks what explains objective moral truth.
moves.warrant: Johnson explicitly grants atheist moral conduct and knowledge, then contrasts brute Platonic ethical facts with God as an explanation.
moves.inference: Harm-based moral knowledge does not by itself answer the metaphysical grounding question.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is Johnson’s complete final rebuttal clarification of the moral argument and its target.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i'm not claiming that atheists can't be moral people they can
moves.attributionRationale: This closes Johnson’s uninterrupted rebuttal before the excluded Q&A.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the central distinction required to represent the moral argument accurately.

burdenContact.rationale: It isolates the existence and source of objective moral truth as the relevant burden.

responseComponents.description: Agrees atheists can be moral while denying that this resolves moral grounding.
Contrasts mind-based assessment with the question of objective truth’s source.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Calling a timeless and spaceless cause powerful imports a physical concept that requires work over time.
moves.warrant: Barker defines power as work over time and asks how an entity outside space and time could possess it.
moves.inference: The cosmological conclusion does not coherently supply the divine attribute of power.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is a self-contained closing objection to the claimed power of the first cause.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: power is work over time
moves.attributionRationale: This is within Barker’s independently introduced formal closing after the excluded interval.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the step from an unexplained cause to a powerful supreme being.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether a stated divine attribute is meaningful under the proposed timeless definition.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the further attribution of physical power to the proposed cause.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A mind is the functioning of a physical brain, not a separate thing requiring transcendent explanation.
moves.warrant: Barker compares mind to bodily functions such as digestion and circulation, which cease when their organs cease functioning.
moves.inference: Inferring an immaterial divine mind from human mental activity commits a category mistake.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Barker’s complete closing response to reifying minds, ending at his stated category-mistake conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the mind is the function of an organism

moves.importanceRationale: It answers the affirmative analogy from human minds to an immaterial designer.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds mental functions in organisms and rejects a separate immaterial explanatory entity.

responseComponents.description: Rejects treating human mental functioning as an immaterial model for a cosmic designer.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The formal case has not connected the evidential steps sufficiently to convince Barker.
moves.warrant: Barker asks whether Johnson filled the stated absences, says he remains unconvinced but open to persuasion, and notes that evil was not developed in this debate.
moves.inference: Qualified nonbelief remains justified on the formal record.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly concludes that the affirmative case has not displaced critical nonbelief.

Maintains that design has not been established.
Maintains that the moral route has not established God.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
